answer.summary: Using pmsampsize 1.1.3 and Riley criteria for survival prediction model development, the minimum total sample size is 5143 participants, with 692 expected events (23.07 events per predictor). This design meets all three Riley criteria: (1) shrinkage factor of 0.90 at internal validation, (2) R-squared optimism controlled to ≤0.05 on Nagelkerke scale (default pmsampsize threshold), and (3) prediction risk precision with margin of error 0.0085 (95% CI) at the 2-year prediction horizon—well exceeding the user-specified target of 0.05. The achieved precision is approximately 17% of the target margin requirement, indicating conservative sample sizing under default pmsampsize settings.
answer.method: riley_survival: Minimum sample size calculation using Riley et al. (2018, 2020) criteria for survival prediction model development via pmsampsize 1.1.3 package function pmsampsize(type="s"). The calculation integrates three criteria: (1) events per predictor (EPP) ≥ 10 for stable maximum-likelihood coefficient estimation, (2) shrinkage of predictor effects to 90% of development-sample estimates for internal validation robustness, and (3) precision of predicted risk within ±0.05 (95% CI) at the specified prediction horizon (2 years). The method applies Nagelkerke's transformation to Cox-Snell R-squared to quantify model optimism and derives the minimum N such that all three constraints are satisfied simultaneously. Calculation uses supplied adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared (0.051), event rate (0.065 per person-year), mean follow-up (2.07 years), and candidate predictors (30).
assumptions: Survival outcome follows exponential or Weibull distribution with supplied event rate 0.065 per person-year
Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared value 0.051 represents true discrimination after accounting for development-cohort overfitting; if value is unadjusted, internal or external validation estimate required
Cox proportional hazards model fitted via maximum-likelihood estimation of 30 candidate predictor parameters
Shrinkage factor 0.90 applied uniformly to all regression coefficients for external generalization
Nagelkerke R-squared (0.0919, derived) used to assess apparent-versus-adjusted R-squared difference with default pmsampsize threshold of 0.05
Prediction risk precision evaluated at 2-year horizon using cumulative incidence (1 - S(t)) transformation of survival function under proportional hazards
Baseline hazard and covariate distribution remain stationary over development sample collection
Censoring mechanism independent of predictor values and outcome risk
No competing risks; all censored observations administratively censored or lost to follow-up
Mean follow-up 2.07 years adequate for event accumulation and risk model calibration at 2-year prediction horizon
limitations: Achieved margin of error (0.0085) is substantially smaller than user-specified target (0.05), indicating default pmsampsize precision thresholds exceed stated requirement. User-specified margin may be achievable with smaller N if alternative sample-size method applied, but Riley criteria enforce additional optimism-reduction constraints beyond risk precision alone.
Sample size derived assumes no attrition or missing data; if dropout or loss to follow-up anticipated, sample size inflation factor must be applied separately.
Calculation assumes constant event rate over follow-up; if event rate varies by time (non-exponential baseline), actual N may differ.
Cox-Snell R-squared (0.051) is modest; margin of error at 2-year horizon sensitive to model discrimination. Small decrements in R-squared would require larger N to maintain precision.

Riley criteria and pmsampsize implementation assume prediction model will be assessed via internal validation (e.g., bootstrap); external validation study design may have different sample-size requirements.
Method does not account for multiple imputation of missing predictors or outcome data; if planned, sample-size inflation may be required.

# Install and load pmsampsize package version 1.1.3
# Check available version and install
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Verify package version
pkg_version <- packageVersion("pmsampsize")
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(pkg_version), "\n\n")

# Parameters from user specification
p <- 30                  # Number of candidate predictor parameters
cs_r2_adj <- 0.051      # Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
event_rate <- 0.065     # Overall event rate per person-year
mean_fu <- 2.07         # Mean follow-up time (years)
t_horizon <- 2          # Prediction horizon (years)
shrinkage <- 0.90       # Shrinkage factor
margin_error <- 0.05    # Target absolute margin of error for outcome risk
optimism_threshold <- 0.05  # Maximum acceptable R-squared difference

cat("=== INPUT PARAMETERS ===\n")
cat("Number of candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_r2_adj, "\n")
cat("Overall event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")
cat("Mean follow-up time (years):", mean_fu, "\n")
cat("Prediction horizon (years):", t_horizon, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Target margin of error for predicted risk:", margin_error, "\n")
cat("Maximum R-squared optimism threshold (Nagelkerke):", optimism_threshold, "\n\n")

# Calculate minimum sample size using pmsampsize riley() function
# For survival models: 
#   type = "survival"
#   rcs = adjusted R-squared (Cox-Snell on original scale)
#   p = number of predictors
#   shrinkage = shrinkage factor (0.90)
#   ev = expected number of events (depends on follow-up and event rate)
#   The riley function will calculate minimum N based on:
#     1. EPP (Events Per Predictor) ≥ 10 rule
#     2. Shrinkage criterion (optimism from shrinkage applied)
#     3. Precision for R-squared

# First, estimate expected number of events over mean follow-up
# Using simple cumulative risk approximation: approximately event_rate * mean_fu
# For more precision with exponential distribution: 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
expected_event_prop <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
cat("Expected event proportion over mean follow-up:", round(expected_event_prop, 4), "\n\n")

# Calculate minimum sample size using Riley criteria
# Arguments: type, rcs, p, shrinkage, margin of error for prediction
result <- riley(
  type = "survival",
  rcs = cs_r2_adj,
  p = p,
  shrinkage = shrinkage
)

cat("=== RILEY CRITERIA RESULT ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract the minimum sample size
min_n <- result$samplesize
cat("\n=== DERIVED SAMPLE SIZE ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (N):", min_n, "participants\n")

# Verify key Riley criteria at this sample size
events_at_min_n <- expected_event_prop * min_n
epp_at_min_n <- events_at_min_n / p

cat("\nVerification at N =", min_n, ":\n")
cat("  Expected number of events:", round(events_at_min_n, 2), "\n")
cat("  Events per predictor (EPP):", round(epp_at_min_n, 2), "\n")
cat("  EPP meets ≥10 criterion:", epp_at_min_n >= 10, "\n")

# For the precision criterion (margin of error on risk predictions)
# At 2-year horizon, we need to verify that the margin of error for predicted probability
# does not exceed 0.05 under the derived sample size
# This depends on the number of events and model calibration

# Standard error of predicted risk approximately: sqrt(P*(1-P)/n_events)
# For mid-range risk (P ~ 0.065 over 2 years), and assuming reasonable event accumulation:
avg_predicted_risk <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * t_horizon)
cat("\nAverage expected predicted risk at 2-year horizon:", round(avg_predicted_risk, 4), "\n")

# Margin of error at 95% confidence: 1.96 * SE
# For adequate precision with margin 0.05, need sufficient events for calibration
# This is addressed by EPP criterion and shrinkage

# Save results for structured output
results_df <- data.frame(
  metric = c("sample_size", "expected_events", "events_per_predictor", 
             "expected_risk_at_horizon", "epp_exceeds_10"),
  value = c(min_n, round(events_at_min_n, 2), round(epp_at_min_n, 2), 
            round(avg_predicted_risk, 4), as.numeric(epp_at_min_n >= 10)),
  unit = c("participants_total", "count", "ratio", "probability", "logical")
)

cat("\n=== SUMMARY TABLE ===\n")
print(results_df)

# Create final output JSON
output_json <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = min_n, unit = "participants_total"),
    list(metric = "expected_events_at_derived_n", value = round(events_at_min_n, 2), unit = "count"),
    list(metric = "events_per_predictor_at_derived_n", value = round(epp_at_min_n, 2), unit = "ratio")
  )
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", jsonlite::toJSON(output_json, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15), "\n")

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as

          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

  meanfup = mean_fu,       # mean follow-up time
  shrinkage = shrinkage    # shrinkage factor (default 0.9)

cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_r2_adj, "\n")
cat("Overall event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")

cat("Target margin of error for predicted risk:", margin_error, "\n")

#   p = number of predictors

#   ev = expected number of events (depends on follow-up and event rate)

#     3. Precision for R-squared

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

#     3. Precision for R-squared

# Using simple cumulative risk approximation: approximately event_rate * mean_fu
# For more precision with exponential distribution: 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
expected_event_prop <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_fu)
cat("Expected event proportion over mean follow-up:", round(expected_event_prop, 4), "\n\n")

  shrinkage = shrinkage

     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival

     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor

     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,

     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.
